# Bioresorbable Vascular Scaffolds in Percutaneous Coronary Intervention: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

The evolution of percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) has been marked by successive technological breakthroughs, from balloon angioplasty to bare-metal stents (BMS) and subsequently drug-eluting stents (DES) [1]. Despite the substantial reductions in restenosis and target-lesion revascularization achieved by DES, concerns persisted regarding the permanent presence of a metallic implant, including chronic inflammation, impaired vasomotion, late stent thrombosis, and the inability to perform future surgical revascularization [2,3]. Bioresorbable vascular scaffolds (BVS) emerged as a conceptually appealing solution, intended to provide transient mechanical support during vessel healing before complete resorption, theoretically restoring native vascular physiology [4].

## Concept and Device Design

The dominant BVS technology has been the poly-L-lactic acid (PLLA) platform, exemplified by the Absorb everolimus-eluting scaffold (Abbott Vascular) [5]. PLLA degrades through hydrolysis of ester bonds into lactic acid, ultimately metabolized via the Krebs cycle to carbon dioxide and water, with complete resorption typically occurring over two to three years [6]. Other approaches included magnesium-based scaffolds (Magmaris), which offered favorable mechanical properties and faster resorption [7]. The theoretical advantages of these devices included the restoration of cyclic pulsatility, late lumen enlargement, plaque regression, and freedom from a permanent nidus for thrombosis [8].

## Pivotal Clinical Evidence

Early first-in-human studies and the ABSORB cohort series demonstrated feasibility, with evidence of restored vasomotion and scaffold resorption on intravascular imaging [9,10]. These encouraging signals led to larger randomized trials. The ABSORB II trial compared the Absorb scaffold with the Xience cobalt-chromium everolimus-eluting stent and initially showed comparable clinical outcomes, though it failed to meet its co-primary endpoints of superior vasomotion and lower late lumen loss [11,12]. ABSORB III, the largest pivotal trial, demonstrated noninferiority for target-lesion failure at one year but raised concern with numerically higher device thrombosis [13]. ABSORB Japan and ABSORB China provided consistent short-term efficacy data supporting regulatory approval [14,15].

However, longer-term follow-up reshaped the clinical narrative. Pooled and individual-patient meta-analyses revealed a significantly increased risk of scaffold thrombosis, particularly between one and three years, coinciding with the resorption phase [16,17]. The AIDA trial confirmed higher rates of definite or probable device thrombosis with Absorb compared with Xience in routine practice [18]. Three-year outcomes from ABSORB II showed inferior vasomotor reactivity and a higher rate of target-vessel myocardial infarction [19], while ABSORB III three-year data confirmed excess target-lesion failure and thrombosis [20].

## Mechanisms of Failure

Investigations into the causes of adverse events highlighted several factors. The relatively thick struts (approximately 150 µm) of first-generation scaffolds protruded into the lumen, predisposing to flow disturbance and thrombosis [21]. Scaffold discontinuities during resorption, malapposition, and uncovered struts were implicated in late events [22]. Crucially, suboptimal implantation technique—including inadequate lesion preparation, undersizing, and insufficient postdilation—was associated with worse outcomes, prompting the development of the "PSP" (predilation, sizing, postdilation) optimized implantation strategy [23,24]. Intravascular imaging guidance was emphasized to mitigate these risks [25].

## Regulatory and Clinical Status

In light of accumulating safety data, Abbott Vascular withdrew the Absorb BVS from the commercial market in 2017 [26]. Professional society statements subsequently recommended caution and restricted use [27]. Despite this setback, magnesium-based scaffolds continued clinical investigation, with the BIOSOLVE program demonstrating acceptable safety and lower thrombosis rates, suggesting that platform composition and strut design are critical determinants of outcome [7,28].

## Future Directions

The BVS experience has provided enduring lessons for cardiovascular device development [29]. Next-generation scaffolds aim for thinner struts, improved radial strength, faster and more predictable resorption, and enhanced deliverability. Ongoing research explores novel polymers, refined metallic alloys, and improved drug-elution kinetics, coupled with mandatory imaging-guided optimal implantation [30]. Whether these refinements can deliver on the original promise of "vascular restoration therapy" while matching the safety of contemporary thin-strut DES remains to be established through rigorous long-term randomized trials [29,30].

## Conclusion

Bioresorbable vascular scaffolds represented a paradigm shift in interventional cardiology, predicated on the elegant concept of transient mechanical support followed by complete resorption. While early data were promising, longer-term randomized evidence revealed an excess of scaffold thrombosis and target-lesion failure relative to best-in-class metallic DES, attributable to device design limitations and implantation technique. Although the first-generation Absorb device was withdrawn, the field continues to evolve. The central challenge remains balancing the theoretical biological advantages of resorption against the demonstrated need for durable, thin-strut mechanical performance.
